financial_summary: Postal Realty Trust, Inc. is a small-cap real estate business with a $955M market cap on $96M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +22% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder. Operating margins are expanding by +5.9pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 3% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $38M in free cash flow — roughly 39 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 6.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.3× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Net dilution runs at 1.7% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 3.9% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 36% operating margin runs 13pp above the Real Estate median (23%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 53% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 12% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $20.57 (margin of safety -8%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $13.15 to $31.54 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Real Estate peers: P/E 38.9 vs 23.6 and P/FCF 25.4 vs 17.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 47% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.9% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 7 covering analysts target $26.07 on average, 18% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 3% falls short of the cost of capital of 6.8%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.53).
It converts 39% of revenue into free cash flow, or 33% after stock compensation.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 3.15x.
AFFO margin (a proxy for distributable REIT cash) is 39%.
ROE of 5% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.7x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 18pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 6.2x net debt to EBITDA ($1.5M of cash against $361.1M of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.3x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.57 in the distress zone, which caps the rating at HOLD.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 21.6% over 3 years and 31.2% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 35%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 34.8% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: FFO growth of 36.5% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.3x depreciation (7.2% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.9%, and institutions hold 75%.
Net share issuance leaves shareholder yield negative (-1.7%), diluting holders.
The share count has grown 19.6% a year over five years, diluting existing holders.
It pays out 171% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 13.1% of the float, 10.8 days to cover.
